newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Yugo M1 rises in April but dinar seen stable.
newsitem.headline: Yugo M1 rises in April but dinar seen stable.

text.p: Yugoslavia's M1 money supply rose in April to 5.562 billion dinars ($974 million) from 5.289 billion in March, but economists said on Thursday the increase will not immediately affect prices or the dinar market rate.

"You can't say when this monetary expansion is going to translate into higher prices or hit the dinar, there is always a time lag between the actual monetary expansion and its effects," Stojan Stamenkovic of the Institute of Economic Sciences told reporters.

A similar monetary expansion last December when the M1 grew to 5.495 billion dinars from 5.042 billion in one month pushed the dinar black market rate to 4.3 to the German mark, its lowest since 1994.

Fears that the dinar black market rate may begin to fall again after resting at 3.5 to the German mark for weeks now, appeared after unconfirmed reports leaked to the press that M1 has exceeded six billion dinars in May.
The central bank issues its money supply figures with two-three months delay.
"It makes little difference whether the M1 is at six billion dinars or lower. The main thing is that such monetary expansion will sooner or later result in higher prices," an economist said.

"This definitely shows that the central bank has departed from its restrictive monetary policy which may have serious consequences," Slobodan Milosavljevic of the IZIT Institute for Market Research told Reuters.
"But this is not such a dramatic increase to immediately produce consequences," he added.

Economists agreed that part of the increase in the M1 monetary aggregate in April may have resulted from a growing inflow of remittances from Yugoslavs working abroad and to a lesser extent from export earnings.
But Stamenkovic cautioned there were no such dollar earnings justifying this big monthly increase in the M1.
Economists also said the latest increase in the M1 money supply had been done very carefully and very wisely.

"The money must have ended in paying all those overdue pensions and wages to public sector workers, but they have spent all of it in advance and the government knew the money will be used to pay rent and electricity, so the money ends up with the state one way or the other," another economist said.

Analysts cautioned expanding money supply could indicate that some funds were used to finance non-priority activities, such as the pre-election campaign ahead of republican parliament and presidential elections due later this year. -- Gordana Filipovic, Belgrade newsroom, +381 11 222 4254
